facts.claim: "John Wayne [Feat. Buzzy Lee]" is track 4 on Denzel Curry's album Melt My Eyez See Your Future, released 25 March 2022, and runs 2:36.
The album is released through PH Recordings under exclusive license to Loma Vista Recordings, a Concord Label Group release.
JPEGMAFIA produced "John Wayne". Discogs lists the writers as B. Hendricks (JPEGMAFIA), D. Curry and S. Spielberg (Buzzy Lee).
Buzzy Lee is the stage name of Sasha Spielberg.
JPEGMAFIA does not rap on the track. Buzzy Lee's vocals open it.
The album was recorded at The Brewery, Electric Lady Studios and Quad Recording Studios. Nathan Burgess recorded and mixed it, and Chris Gehringer mastered it at Sterling Sound.

The song addresses police brutality, gun culture and the cyclical nature of violence. It opens with a gunshot, and the "John Wayne" of the chorus is a metaphor for carrying a gun for self-defense against corrupt cops.

In a March 2022 Loud and Quiet interview, Curry said he feels he must carry a weapon to protect himself from the people who are supposed to protect him. The subject comes with personal experience: his brother Treon "Lotto Tree" Johnson died after being tased by police in 2014.

Loud and Quiet says Curry wrote the album title in his notepad on 2 September 2018, and returned to it after finishing 2019's Zuu. It calls JPEGMAFIA one of the few collaborators Curry kept close contact with during the pandemic.
The video for the album's lead single "Walkin" ends with Curry facing an actor credited as "John Wayne".

Denzel Curry is a rapper from Carol City, Miami Gardens, Florida. He first gained attention when SpaceGhostPurrp shared his mixtape King Remembered Underground Tape 1991-1995, which led to his membership in Raider Klan.

research.lineage: The song sits in socially conscious, politically charged hip-hop from Curry's Florida underground roots, with experimental production from JPEGMAFIA, on an album that mixes traditional hip-hop, jazz and other genres Curry grew up on.

draft:
**John Wayne** begins in the middle of a sentence. Buzzy Lee's opening lines drift through something soft and battered, settling on a bare admission of how hard it's been, then break off mid-comparison. Denzel Curry's hook finishes the thought: he walks around the hood like John Wayne. The man who played the American lawman on screen becomes the costume a young Black man wears to survive the actual law.

The song is about the police, and Curry has said so plainly. He told Loud and Quiet he feels he has to carry a weapon to protect himself from the people who are supposed to protect him. That fear has a source: his brother Treon "Lotto Tree" Johnson died after being tased by police in 2014. Hear the verses with that in mind and the bravado shows its seams. "911, emergency will murder me the day I call 'em" is a threat on the surface and terror underneath. When he admits "So much pain I've endured, now I'm painless," the boast is really numbness, a scar he has decided to call armor.

The chorus holds the knot that never comes loose. "I'ma give them what they gave us on the first grade" turns revenge into something old and childish, a debt that started on the playground and never stopped compounding. It's pride and grief at once. In the second verse he says his little weapon gave him power when he aimed it, which is as honest as the song gets about what the gun means. It's less protection than the first time he felt anything but small. He even hedges in the middle of a kill-or-be-killed line with a shrugging "I guess," and that small word carries more doubt than any of the swagger around it.

JPEGMAFIA, one of the few collaborators Curry stayed close to through the pandemic, built the beat. It's dry and close: a drum machine with a hard snare, a bass pattern that repeats without relief, and high synths hanging above it all. Curry raps fast and sure on top, with nothing to blur his edges. The cleanliness is the point. There's no reverb to hide in. The track also carries an echo of the video for the album's lead single "Walkin," which ends with Curry facing an actor credited as "John Wayne."

This is the Carol City kid who came up through SpaceGhostPurrp's Raider Klan, now aiming his old underground aggression at a larger target. The hook keeps saying "we sing," turning one man's armed vigil into a chant for everyone in the struggle. Then the song ends on a curse at a world that's already lying.

It sticks because the chorus makes you shout along with a revenge fantasy before you notice it's really a confession of fear.
